opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something we spent a lot of time on, and the answer surprised us a bit at first. The default intuition is that you should always distill from the strongest model you can afford. But once you fix the compute budget, that framing is incomplete, because a smaller model is much cheaper per sample. For the same FLOPs you might get several times more solutions out of a weaker model than out of a stronger one.

So you have to think about three things together. First is coverage: how many unique problems end up with at least one correct solution. Second is diversity: how many distinct correct reasoning paths you get per problem. Third is the false positive rate: how often you get the right final answer through flawed reasoning.

When you sample a lot more from the smaller model, coverage and diversity often go up quite a bit. You solve more of the hard tail of problems simply because you get more attempts, and you see more varied ways of solving each one. The cost is that the weaker model tends to have a higher false positive rate, so some of those "correct" traces have sloppy reasoning in them.

What we found is that, at least for reasoning tasks like math, the coverage and diversity gains often outweigh the extra noise. Models fine-tuned on the compute-matched data from the weaker, cheaper model frequently did better than ones trained on fewer samples from the stronger model. That held across a few setups: standard knowledge distillation, self-improvement, and even a setting where a weaker model's data helps train a stronger student, which we started calling weak-to-strong improvement.

The practical takeaway is to compare at matched compute rather than matched number of samples. And if you have a good verifier, or can filter the reasoning and not just the final answer, the smaller-teacher strategy gets even stronger, because you're cutting down the main downside. The gap between small and large models is also shrinking, so I'd expect this to matter more over time, not less.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we looked at pretty carefully, and the answer surprised a lot of people, including me a bit. The intuition most folks have is: use the biggest, strongest model you can afford as the teacher, because better model, better data. And if you're comparing one sample from a big model against one sample from a small model, sure, the big model's sample is better. But that's not the comparison you actually face when the budget is fixed.

The right way to frame it is compute-matched. If your budget is some fixed number of FLOPs for generation, a model that's, say, ten times smaller gives you roughly ten times as many samples per problem. So the question becomes: would you rather have one high-quality solution per problem from Gemma 27B, or something like ten or more solutions per problem from Gemma 9B, or thirty from 2B? And what we found is that for reasoning tasks like MATH and GSM8K, the smaller, weaker teacher wins when you're compute-matched, and it wins pretty consistently across the different finetuning setups we tried: knowledge distillation, self-improvement, and this weak-to-strong setup where the small model is generating data for a bigger student.

The reason comes down to a few properties of the data. The first is coverage. With many more samples, you end up solving more unique problems. The strong model might nail the easy problems with one shot, but the hard problems are the ones you actually want in your training set, and with enough samples the weaker model gets some of those right too. The second is diversity. Multiple correct solutions per problem means the student sees different reasoning paths, which matters a lot for generalization. And the third is the cost side, which is the false positive rate. Weaker models produce more solutions where the final answer is right but the reasoning is wrong somewhere in the middle. That's the real risk, and it's why you need good filtering. We found the false positive rate was somewhat higher for the smaller teacher but not dramatically so, and the coverage and diversity gains more than made up for it.

There's a caveat I'd put on all this. It depends on having a verifier. For math, you can check the final answer against ground truth, so the filtering is cheap and reliable. If you're in a domain where you can't verify, then you're leaning entirely on the generator's quality, and the strong model's advantage comes back. So my mental model is: if you can verify, bias toward the weaker, cheaper model and sample a lot. If you can't, the calculus shifts.

The other thing I'd add is that this is partly a statement about where the frontier is at a given moment. The "weak" model today is a very capable model by last year's standards. So "weak" here is relative to the budget, not an absolute claim that bad data is good data. It's really a claim that at fixed compute, breadth of coverage and diversity are worth more than per-sample polish, as long as you have a way to throw out the junk.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about it as a quality-versus-quantity tradeoff. With a fixed budget, a larger teacher might give you better examples, but you get fewer of them. A smaller teacher lets you generate more data, cover more inputs, or sample multiple answers for each input.

The thing I’d optimize for is the student’s performance, rather than the teacher’s performance in isolation. If the smaller teacher can already solve the tasks you care about reliably, more coverage might be more valuable than a marginal improvement in answer quality. If it consistently gets the important reasoning wrong, generating more of those answers won’t help.

So I’d spend a small part of the budget on a controlled comparison: generate data from each teacher at the same dollar cost, train the student, and evaluate on held-out tasks. You could also use the smaller teacher for easier examples and reserve the larger teacher for the harder ones. There isn’t a universal winner; it depends on where better supervision actually changes what the student learns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it as a quality-versus-quantity tradeoff. With a fixed generation budget, a smaller teacher can give you more examples, while a larger teacher can give you fewer but potentially better examples. The question is which dataset helps your student learn more.

That depends on the task and where the student is today. If the smaller teacher can already produce reliable answers, generating more diverse examples may be more valuable than paying for a stronger teacher. But if you’re working on harder reasoning problems where the smaller teacher frequently gets things wrong, more data might just mean more incorrect supervision.

So I’d run a small, controlled experiment: spend the same generation budget on each teacher, train the same student, and evaluate on the tasks you care about. Teacher capability alone isn’t the metric—you want student improvement per dollar.
